newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMANY SEES HOPE AS FLOOD SURGE FAILS TO COME.
newsitem.headline: GERMANY SEES HOPE AS FLOOD SURGE FAILS TO COME.

text.p: Floods along the River Oder on the German-Polish border showed signs of receding on Wednesday after a fresh high-water surge expected overnight did not materialise, officials in east Germany said.
But officials warned that the situation remained critical because the dikes were extremely porous and riddled with weak spots.

Thousands of soldiers, aid workers and villagers have been sandbagging around the clock since last week in a spectacular effort to prop up sections of water-sodden flood barriers reinforcing the banks of the surging river.

Some of the worst floods this century have hit Poland and the Czech Republic this month, claiming more than 100 lives. No deaths have been reported in Germany but homes, businesses and farms have been extensively damaged.
"We were expecting much worse," Alwin Ziel, the interior minister of the regional state of Brandenburg, said of the surge which had been feared overnight.
"Water levels could fall considerably by Thursday," another Brandenburg official said, offering hope to thousands of Germans who live along the river.

But Ziel told Berlin's InfoRadio that despite drier weather in neighbouring Poland and the Czech Republic, where floods have devasted large swathes of farmland, the worst may not yet be over for Germany.

As a precaution, local officials plan mass inoculations this week, fearing that rotting animal carcasses could bring disease to flooded towns south of Frankfurt an der Oder where hundreds of houses are submerged to the rooftops.
Ziel said that despite the programme there was no real risk, and dismissed rumours that drinking water was polluted.
"We have no problems at all (with polluted water) at present and I do not expect such problems in the future," he said.

About 900 soldiers fought overnight to support a critical section of a dike on a 70-km stretch of river along the low-lying Oderbruch region, where some 5,000 of the 19,000 inhabitants were evacuated last week.

Oderbruch, once the bread basket of the former communist East Germany, was drained 250 years ago to create fertile farmland and is vulnerable to flooding because it lies lower than the river, which is held back by dikes.
The Oder dikes have not failed since 1947, when floods wrought havoc around the town of Reitwein, north of Frankfurt an der Oder.
Local officials said damage to agricultural land was already worse than they had anticipated and there were signs the European Union was willing to send aid.

"I think there is a great readiness in Brussels to help us and I have great hopes that we can expect substantial aid, particularly in the agricultural sector," Brandenburg's farm minister Edwin Zimmermann told InfoRadio.
European Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies was expected to announce EU aid to German flood victims later on Wednesday.
